Description
A PhD studentship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/). The student will lead a research project on the population ecology of Greenland white-fronted geese, using 40-year data sets to address long-standing questions about drivers of productivity on breeding areas and subpopulation structure. 
 The Greenland white-fronted goose population has continued to decline, from a peak of 35,000 individuals in 1999 to 13,000 individuals in 2025. Productivity is the proximate mechanism for population change and there is continued uncertainty about the degree to which breeding conditions explain variation in productivity. Further, there are ~45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks (subpopulations) with hypothesized differential demographic structure contributing to the decline and winter range contraction. This PhD studentship has been developed to encourage discovery with anticipated conservation application. Our project goals are to (1) estimate the environmental drivers on breeding areas of productivity in Greenland white-fronted geese, (2) identify structure in survival and reproductive success among 45 wintering Greenland white-fronted goose flocks, and (3) connect population and individual processes linking demography with individual movement and behaviour. The student will use data from thousands of neck-collared individuals and hundreds of GPS-tagged individuals spanning 40 years. This project is an international partnership among National Parks and Wildlife Service (Ireland), Aarhus University (Denmark) and University of Saskatchewan (Canada). There will be substantial additional opportunities for the student to collaborate on other projects in population and movement ecology.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have an MSc and undergraduate degree in ecology, statistics or a closely related field, and interpersonal skills to lead discussions among collaborators. Preference will be given to those with a strong quantitative background (e.g., experience with Program R, Bayesian methods) and knowledge of migratory bird ecology and management. Students must have a valid driver’s license. The successful applicant will be expected to publish manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals and present papers at scientific meetings.

Graduate Student Opportunities in Urban Animal Cognition and Behavior

Dr. Lauren Stanton | Department of Biological Sciences | Illinois State University
Our research group investigates how animals perceive, learn about, and respond to the challenges and opportunities of living in human-altered environments. We are particularly interested in how individual differences shape wildlife responses to urbanization, influence human-wildlife interactions, and inform coexistence strategies. Looking forward, we will explore how early life experiences, social learning, and cultural transmission further shape animal behavior within and across cities. 

We value partnerships with local communities and recognize community science and public engagement as necessary for not only understanding urban wildlife, but also for the development of effective, equitable approaches to human-wildlife coexistence.


Current Research Opportunities
Graduate students will contribute to an ongoing research program investigating the behavior and ecology of urban raccoons (Procyon lotor) in San Francisco, California. This Bay Area Raccoon Project includes a substantial existing dataset, providing opportunities to investigate questions related to urban animal physiology, health, behavior, cognition, social interactions, movement, and space use.

MS Student (1 position)
The MS student will primarily use existing GPS and biologging data from the Bay Area Raccoon Project for their thesis chapters. This position is particularly well suited to someone interested in asking novel questions by integrating behavioral, animal telemetry, and geospatial datasets.

Potential research topics include individual- and neighborhood-level differences in raccoon activity, health, and risk-taking behavior. The student will work closely with existing collaborators to develop focused, independent research questions using available data. 

Previous research or field experience is expected (see more below). Basic familiarity with R and statistical analyses is required. Additional experience with data analysis, GIS, writing, or science communication is highly desirable. 

 
PhD Student (1 position)
The PhD student will contribute to the existing Bay Area Raccoon Project as part of their dissertation (1–2 chapters), while also developing new, independent investigations (2–3 additional chapters).

Experimental investigations will likely involve additional fieldwork and data collection with raccoons in San Francisco, although opportunities to develop complementary research in Illinois, or with other species, may also be possible. The student will have substantial opportunities to develop independent research questions and pursue work at the intersection of animal behavior, cognition, urban ecology, and human-wildlife interactions.

Experience developing hypotheses, conducting independent research, analyzing data, and communicating findings through presentations or publications is expected. Proficiency in R and experience with statistical analyses are strongly preferred. A publication, manuscript in preparation, or other evidence of research productivity is highly desirable. See below for additional details.

 Who Should Apply?
We are looking for motivated, creative, and collaborative students with demonstrated experience working in research or applied animal settings. Competitive applicants will have some combination of the following:

Research interests: A strong interest in animal cognition, as well as wildlife behavior, movement ecology, urban ecology, and conservation biology.
Research experience: Previous experience in an academic research laboratory, field research project, or a related setting.
Animal experience: Experience working with animals in a field, zoo, wildlife rehabilitation center, veterinary clinic, or similar professional setting.
Quantitative skills: Basic knowledge of R and statistics, with some understanding of multivariate analyses. Experience or interest in developing skills in machine learning, GIS/spatial analyses, and computational approaches to classifying animal behavior from biologging data is highly desirable.
Communication: Strong written, verbal, and interpersonal skills, with the ability to communicate effectively with both academic and non-academic audiences (e.g., when engaging with the public). Organizational and leadership skills are also desirable. We especially value individuals who are enthusiastic, collaborative, and bring curiosity to their work.
 

How to Apply

A CV or resume.
A brief statement describing their research interests, relevant experience, quantitative skills, and reasons for wanting to join the lab. Please indicate whether you are applying for the MS or PhD position.
Contact information for 3 references.

Please state “Application for ISU graduate position” in the email subject line

Application review will begin immediately, and selected candidates will formally apply to the graduate program by February 1, 2027. Additional information about graduate studies at Illinois State University can be found here: https://illinoisstate.edu/academics/graduate

Two MS Graduate Research Assistantships are available starting May 2026 in the PEASE Lab (peaselab.com) at Southern Illinois University to continue our statewide wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) ecology and management project. One student will lead efforts on gobbling chronology, and the other student will lead efforts on nesting phenology. The students will be co-advised by Drs. Brent Pease and Guillaume Bastille-Rousseau at Southern Illinois University.

One student will focus on wild turkey gobbling chronology. The student will lead field efforts using autonomous recording units (ARUs) to document spatial and/or temporal variation in gobbling chronology (e.g., Kreh et al., 2023 Wildlife Society Bulletin). The focus of this research is to assess timing of male gobbling across Illinois to determine whether current spring harvest season regulations (e.g., timing, zoning, and length of spring harvest seasons) are aligned with timing of gobbling and then provide regulatory recommendations. Addition work will focus on identifying environmental drivers of variation in gobbling chronology as well as methodological work in ARUs, species identification from audio recordings, and/or continued ongoing work within our lab on population estimation (e.g., abundance) via ARU recordings.

One student will focus on wild turkey nesting phenology. The student will lead trapping efforts to tag hens with GPS transmitters to document spatial and/or temporal variation in nesting phenology as well as spatial ecology of turkeys in southern Illinois. Primary field duties include capture and affixing GPS radiotags, monitoring hen survival and nesting and brooding success, and identifying local and landscape factors contributing to movement patterns. Research will emphasize general spatial ecology and population ecology (e.g., movement, space-use, survival, etc.).

This is a well-funded, multi-agency research project, and the graduate students will be expected to assist in hiring and managing field technicians to support the data collection efforts. Additionally, although research questions will be unique among the selected students, their field work will be complimentary, and all individuals will be expected to contribute to all wild turkey research activities carried out. The successful applicants will have (1) obtained B.S. degree in wildlife, ecology, biology, forestry, zoology, or related fields; (2) knowledge of wild turkey ecology; (3) interest in developing quantitative skills with experience using a variety of data types and models; (4) interest in developing knowledge of program R and spatial software (e.g., QGIS, ArcGIS); (5) a driver's license and ability to conduct independent field work in difficult conditions (e.g., steep terrain, poison ivy, ticks); (6) strong oral and written communication skills, and (7) a cooperative, team-oriented mindset eager to carry out wildlife research and address key problems in wildlife conservation and management.

APHIS' mission also includes addressing issues such as wildlife damage and disease management; regulation of genetically engineered crops and animal welfare; and protection of public health and safety as well as natural resources that are vulnerable to invasive pests and pathogens.

Research Project: You will be a part of the National Wildlife Research Center’s (NWRC) Chronic Wasting Disease Project aimed at delivering research products that protect producers and natural resources from wildlife diseases and damage. You will gain experience with the continued development and implementation of a multistate adaptive management framework for white-tailed deer by colaborating with state wildlife agencies, researchers, and other partners to develop and operationalize a collaborative, cross-jurisdiction experimental approach. You will also help with developing data-sharing agreements and ensuring that experimental interventions and evaluation procedures are scientifically rigorous, logistically feasible, consistently implemented, and capable of supporting regional learning and adaptive management of CWD and deer populations. Additionally, you may have opportunities to contribute to other NWRC-led research activities, including, but not limited to, wildlife immobilization, animal sampling and handling, postmortem examinations, and laboratory-based analyses, including diagnostic assays and other bench techniques used to support wildlife disease research.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Contribute to the National Wildlife Research Center’s Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) Project, learn about research that protects agricultural producers, wildlife, and natural resources.
Gain experience developing and implementing a multistate adaptive-management framework for white-tailed deer and CWD.
Collaborate with state wildlife agencies, researchers, and other partners to operationalize cross-jurisdictional management experiments.
Learn to support development of data-sharing agreements and coordinated research processes across multiple agencies and states.
Help ensure that management interventions, monitoring methods, and evaluation procedures are scientifically rigorous, logistically feasible, and consistently implemented.
Develop skills in analyzing and applying data to support regional learning, adaptive management, and decision-making for deer populations and CWD.
Potentially gain hands-on experience in wildlife immobilization, animal handling, biological sampling, and postmortem examinations.
Build laboratory and diagnostic skills through participation in assays and other bench techniques supporting wildlife-disease research.
The research will provide training in ecological and epidemiological data collection; integrating ecological and epidemiological components with concurrent human dimensions pilot-study efforts; and data repository design to support long-term data sharing and analysis across collaborating agencies.

We are inviting applications from early career terrestrial mammal ecologists / conservation biologists for a 3-year Postdoctoral Fellowship being offered in the Applied Behavioural Ecology and Ecosystem Research Unit (ABEERU) at the University of South Africa (UNISA) involving a collaborative research project with the Department of Zoology and Entomology and the Eugène Marais Chair of Wildlife Management at the University of Pretoria.

The successful candidate will be expected to coordinate the initiation and implementation of component research projects investigating the ecology and structure of the small- and medium-sized carnivore assemblage in the Tswalu Kalahari Reserve. ·        A track record of peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations that emanate from their research. 
·        Experience in the capture and monitoring of carnivores.
·        Experience in the deployment of camera traps and the analysis of the resultant data.
·        Advanced GIS and quantitative skills.
·        A valid driver’s licence (and experience operating 4 x 4 vehicles in an off-road setting)
·        Willingness to work in remote locations with minimal direct supervision. 

Responsibilities

·        Submission of at least three peer-reviewed publications per annum.
·        Presentation of research findings at one conference (typically the Oppenheimer Research Conference) per annum.
·        Quarterly reporting on activities and progress with outputs. 
·        Assist with field data collection and analyses (existing/new projects).
·        Co-supervision of postgraduate students.
·        Development of own research project (incl. writing of grant proposal, ethical clearance, etc.) 

Affiliation and application

The successful candidate will be affiliated to ABEERU within the Department of Environmental Sciences, UNISA, and will be hosted jointly by Professor L.R. Brown and Dr H. Melville.

The Southeastern Cooperative Wildlife Disease Study (SCWDS) and the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources at the University of Georgia (UGA), in close collaboration with the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR), are recruiting a Ph.D. student to lead a comprehensive, field-intensive research program investigating the epidemiological, demographic, and behavioral impacts of sarcoptic mange (Sarcoptes scabiei) on American black bear (Ursus americanus) populations in West Virginia. This project builds upon West Virginia's long-term black bear research foundation to support evidence-based management and to better understand the impacts of sarcoptic mange in black bears.
Key Research Objectives & Scope of Work
·         Longitudinal Disease Tracking and Clinical Evaluations 
·         Mortality and Pathological Assessment
·         Demographic and Reproductive Monitoring
·         Movement Ecology and GPS Telemetry
·         Non-Invasive Camera Trap Arrays and Density Estimation

We seek a highly motivated, resilient candidate with strong quantitative abilities, excellent field skills, and a commitment to wildlife disease ecology and population management to join a team of graduate students working on the project.

·         Minimum cumulative undergraduate/graduate GPA >= 3.0 on a 4.0 scale. 
·         Demonstrated experience conducting wildlife field research, animal capture/handling, and data collection. 
·         Physical capability and willingness to perform strenuous, physically demanding fieldwork in rugged, mountainous terrain under adverse weather conditions.
·         Proficiency and demonstrated aptitude in R programming, spatial analysis (GIS), and quantitative methods in natural resources management. 
·         A valid driver's license and clean driving record.
Preferred Qualifications:
·         Direct experience with chemical immobilization and handling of large mammals, preferably black bears or other carnivores.
·         Experience designing and maintaining remote camera trap grids and analyzing camera data.
·         Prior background in telemetry analysis, movement ecology, spatial statistics, and/or Bayesian hierarchical modeling.
·         Familiarity or interest in learning wildlife diagnostic procedures, necropsy, tissue sampling, parasitology, or health assessments.
·         Proven leadership skills managing field technician crews, coordinating field logistics, and communicating effectively with field team and agency partners. 
·         Demonstrated track record of scientific writing, including peer-reviewed publications and oral presentations.

Field research will be conducted across two study regions in West Virginia around Hardy and Pendleton, Pocahontas & Greenbrier counties. Description
The Department of Zoology and Physiology at the University of Wyoming invites applications for the Strickland Family Fish and Wildlife Biometrics Endowed Professorship at the rank of Assistant Professor.  We seek an innovative individual who will develop a collaborative, externally-funded research program that tackles fundamental and applied questions in areas such as hierarchical modeling, statistical study design, population estimation and modeling (e.g., capture-mark-recapture, occupancy, survival) or other quantitatively rigorous area of wildlife and fisheries ecology, or the statistical analyses of complex ecological datasets – with a focus on terrestrial and/or aquatic vertebrates. Importantly, we seek a colleague who moves fluidly between developing new statistical methods, asking fundamental ecological questions, and applying them to pressing wildlife and fisheries management problems or questions at the local (i.e., state of Wyoming), regional, and/or international levels. The successful individual will be expected to contribute to the academic, service, and teaching missions of the Department of Zoology and Physiology, our Wildlife and Fisheries Biology and Management degree, the interdepartmental Ph.D. Program in Ecology and Evolution (PiEE), and more broadly to the University of Wyoming.  Teaching responsibilities may include undergraduate and graduate courses such as ecological statistics, research study design, quantitative methods for wildlife and fisheries (including the development and application of innovative approaches to analyzing ecological data), core courses within the Wildlife and Fisheries Biology and Management major, and/or a new course in the successful applicant’s specialty. The candidate will be expected to participate in appropriate service activities including, but not limited to, serving on departmental, college, and university committees, serving on graduate committees, and providing statistical innovation and support on collaborative grants and research. Candidates are expected to demonstrate a commitment to inclusive, evidence-based teaching and effective mentoring of students from a range of backgrounds and knowledge.

PhD in Applied Statistics, Biological or Ecological Statistics, Wildlife or Fisheries Ecology (with clear emphasis on developing innovative statistical methods), or related field
Experience publishing in peer-reviewed journals
Experience or demonstrated interest in teaching undergraduate- and graduate-level courses
Demonstrated history or strong interest in conducting research in one or more of the following areas: hierarchical modeling, statistical study design, or another quantitatively rigorous area of wildlife and fisheries ecology (e.g., population modeling)

Experience in developing innovative statistical or modeling approaches

Experience and commitment to excellence in research through multiple first-author publications, including in high-impact journals

Research Project: With thousands of commercial chemicals entering the environment, traditional animal-reliant safety assessments can no longer keep pace with the demand for rapid hazard and exposure data. To bridge this gap, EPA’s Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention is pioneering in vitro 'New Approach Method' (NAM) testing strategies to enable fast, cost-effective screening, prioritization, and human health risk assessments. This specific internship is deeply anchored within the analytical chemistry foundation necessary to validate and drive these alternative strategies forward.

As an intern on our team, you will gain experience with EPA’s Risk Assessment Support Division by learning about analytical chemistry method development, validation, and execution. Your primary learning objective will be designing robust sample preparation and quantitative analysis procedures to track chemical concentrations and stability within complex in vitro and biochemical assay matrices, specifically targeted at biological perturbations such as endocrine disruption.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will learn to operate and troubleshoot advanced instrumentation, utilizing high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) and liquid/gas chromatography (LC-MS/MS, GC-MS/MS) to generate high-quality, reproducible kinetic profiles. By pairing your rigorous analytical measurements with exposure-dose and toxicokinetic modeling, you will directly enable the team to translate laboratory data into 'equivalent doses,' allowing scientists to compare systemic configurations against anticipated exposure levels to evaluate overall risk (hazard + exposure = risk).

Learning objectives include:

Advanced Method Development & Validation: Gain hands-on experience in designing, optimizing, and validating highly sensitive, selective analytical chemistry methods to extract and quantify trace-level organic chemicals across diverse and challenging biological and cell-culture matrices.
High-Throughput Analytical Instrumentation: Master the operation, calibration, and troubleshooting of advanced instrumentation, including ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with triple-quadrupole and high-resolution mass spectrometers (UHPLC-MS/MS, Q-TOF).
In Vitro Toxicokinetics (IVTK) Characterization: Develop proficiency in calculating chemical parameters, including hepatic metabolic clearance rates, plasma/media protein binding, and chemical stability, which are vital for determining points of departure for endocrine disruption pathways.
Data Analysis Automation & Quality Assurance: Learn to implement automated data processing pipelines for mass spectrometry datasets, apply rigorous QA/QC metrics, and maintain strict data integrity practices matching good laboratory practices (GLP).
Regulatory Integration & Cross-Disciplinary Teamwork: Understand how raw analytical chemistry data directly translates through exposure models to shape EPA screening, prioritization, and toxicological policy decisions, while enhancing collaborative communication across chemical and biological domains.

Paid opportunity for enrolled undergraduates interested in expanding their conservation research experience! 
 The Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation (SMSC) is seeking to fill 10 paid REU positions for Summer 2027 at our NSF-funded REU site titled “Saving Endangered Species and Habitats: Next-generation Education, Research, and Training for Conservation Biologists.” This 10-week REU, held from May 24 to July 30, 2027, will give undergraduate students an opportunity to conduct hands-on, full-time conservation research and gain career-ready skills to improve knowledge of and best management practices for threatened species with the goal of helping to alleviate the global extinction crisis. Undergraduate students who are very excited about a career in conservation, or interested in related disciplines, such as biology, ecology, genetics, physiology, animal behavior, endocrinology, anthropology, and environmental sciences, are encouraged to apply. 
 NSF-REU eligibility:

REU funding is only available for currently enrolled undergraduate students. Undergraduate students who have graduated or will graduate by the time the REU begins (and are no longer enrolled in the university/college) are not eligible to apply.

Website: Home - UGA Deer Lab | Kohl Lab 
Contacts: Marcelo Jorge ([email removed]), Michel Kohl ([email removed]) 
 Description: This position is part of an interdisciplinary project at the University of Georgia (UGA) led by Drs. Kohl and Jorge in the Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources, funded through the Wheatley Interdisciplinary Faculty Seed Grant Program. The project is a collaborative effort involving state wildlife agencies, university partners, and the Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation (RMEF) aimed and understanding how elk habitat management treatments impact nutrition and population vital rates for eastern elk. Through this position you will develop collaborations with agency and RMEF personnel while collecting, cleaning, and analyzing historical treatment data to inform efficient study design and field work logistics planning. This position is not permitted for remote work. Travel will be required to visit field sites. NOTE: This position is only funded for 6 months. 
 Qualifications: Applicants should have an expressed interest in Eastern elk populations, habitat management, genetics, and/or nutrition. Applicants must have completed a Master’s degree in wildlife management or related field and shown a propensity for R coding, GIS, as well as a strong publication record. Exceptional B.S. applicants may be considered with minimum requirements of a Bachelor’s degree GPA >3.0 along with proficiency in R coding, GIS, and statistical analysis. Applicants must be able to pass a UGA background check and driving records check. 
 The Analyst will join a cohesive team of graduate research assistants, postdocs, and P.I.’s within the Kohl Lab and UGA Deer Lab. Because the project will require extensive work with data management and analysis, the student must be comfortable working on a computer developing their statistical analysis and R coding skills. The position start date is negotiable, but must begin January 1, 2027, and funding is available for 6 months with the potential of Ph.D. Assistantship extension contingent on funding and fit beginning August 1 (assuming funding acquisition). For those interested in pursuing a Ph.D. this position provides additional project development time prior to starting the degree program. 
 To be considered for this position, please send a concise cover letter outlining your interests, research background specifically as they relate to this position along with career aspirations. If interested in the possible follow-up PhD position, please note in your cover letter. Also include a sample publication, resume or curriculum vitae; copies of transcripts (unofficial) for all institutions attended; unofficial copies of GRE scores if available; and contact information for 3 professional references (name, email, phone, address) combined into a single PDF file with the file name formatted as lastname_firstname_Data_Analyst to [email removed] and [email removed].  Review of applications will begin Nov 16th . We will be at the wildlife society annual conference in Iowa if you want to discuss the position in person, otherwise feel free to email any question you may have.

Marcelo jorge
[email removed] (preferred contact method)

Position Summary:

One Ecologist/Forestry Researcher (Full-time, 40 hrs/week) position available with Colorado State University (CSU) Center for Environmental Management of Military Lands (CEMML). This position is part of CEMML’s Early-Career Development Program, which helps emerging professionals bridge academic learning and career success through hands-on experience, mentorship, and professional development. To learn more visit: Early-Career Development Program - CEMML.


This is a research focus position. The role will use GIS and remotely sensed data, along with Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) data to characterize, map, model and analyze tree species composition and related forest attributes in a tropical environment. This will aid in understanding forest ecosystem disturbance and resilience.


For full consideration, please apply by Monday, November 16, 2026, 11:59 PM (MT). 


Essential Job Duties:

Combine existing spatial data with additional predictor variables developed as needed, with Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) data to characterize and map spatial gradients in tree species composition and related forest attributes.

Evaluate whether mapped outputs or model derived spatial predictors can reduce uncertainties in FIA estimates of tree species basal area, biomass, or related composition metrics through one or more model assisted estimation approaches.

Link mapped species composition outputs to an existing dataset of fire occurrences to characterize tree species composition where fires occurred, including areas where field surveys of tree species are not available.

Develop a comparison of uncertainties in FIA estimates of species basal area, biomass, or related composition metrics when estimates are based only on FIA plots versus when model assisted estimation uses mapped auxiliary information.

Create maps of model derived species composition gradients, or related composition outputs.

Model derived composition values for places where fires occurred, along with related charts that help characterize the species composition of forests where fires occur.


Decision Making:

Determine and develop appropriate model parameters.

Determine appropriate spatial predictor data sets.


Supervision:

Does not supervise.


Conditions of Employment:

Successful completion of CSU’s standard pre-employment background check.

Minimum Qualifications:

PhD in Systems Ecology or related field, including coursework in ecology, ecosystem climatology, statistics, spatial statistics, machine learning, applied bioinformatics, data visualization, geographic information systems and science communication.

One year experience in systems ecology, including work in GIS and remote sensing and FIA plot data in tropical islands of the US.

Experience as first author publishing a refereed journal article in a top journal focused on research typically requiring geospatial data and analysis (e.g., Remote Sensing or Ecological Indicators).

Experience with programming languages including R and Python.


Preferred Qualifications:

Experience developing spatial or statistical models of forest composition, biomass, basal area, or related ecological attributes.

Experience applying model-assisted estimation or other methods that integrate forest inventory data with auxiliary spatial information.

Experience integrating remote sensing, climate, topographic, fire, or other disturbance data in geospatial analyses.

Advanced proficiency using R, Python, and GIS for spatial modeling, uncertainty analysis, visualization, and reproducible workflows.

Experience communicating geospatial research through peer-reviewed publications, technical reports, maps, or presentations.

Description

Fisheries Ecology Positions

Two contractor opportunities  |  B.S. and M.S. levels

Quantitative and Conservation Ecology Team  •  U.S. Geological Survey  •  Columbia, Missouri

Position Description
The Quantitative and Conservation Ecology (QCE) team at the U.S. Geological Survey Columbia Environmental Research Center is seeking two student-services contractors to support a broad portfolio of freshwater fisheries research. We anticipate hiring one early-career biologist who is nearing completion of, or has recently completed, a B.S. degree and a second biologist who is nearing completion of, or has recently completed, an M.S. degree.

Both individuals will contribute to multiple projects rather than a single assigned study. Research occurs in the Great Lakes, Mississippi River basin, and other river systems, with the balance of field, laboratory, and analytical activities varying by season and project needs.

Research Areas
·  Fish movement and habitat use: acoustic, radio, and PIT telemetry studies examining movement, survival, habitat selection, and connectivity.
·  River restoration and barrier effects: evaluating fish movements and community responses to dam removal, passage improvements, and other restoration actions, including work in the Cuyahoga River watershed.
·  Invasive species and fisheries sampling: invasive carp monitoring and removal, gear comparisons, sampling efficiency, and standardized fish surveys in large rivers and tributaries.
·  Population and community ecology: assessment of fish distributions, occupancy, abundance, survival, and recruitment using field observations and quantitative approaches.
·  Methods development and experimental research: side-scan sonar, habitat mapping, controlled field or pond experiments, and complementary monitoring techniques.

Types of Services Required

Field Activities

·  Deploy, maintain, and retrieve acoustic receivers, PIT equipment, radio telemetry systems, and other monitoring gear.
·  Conduct active fish tracking and standardized field sampling from boats, kayaks, and shorelines using appropriate sampling gear.
·  Collect biological and environmental measurements, maintain field records, and assist with fish handling and sample processing.
·  Participate in gear evaluation trials, habitat surveys, and aquatic research experiments.
·  Operate or learn to operate small vessels, trailers, and field equipment safely; participate in overnight and multi-day field assignments as required by the position.


Data, Laboratory, and Research Activities

·  Download, organize, verify, and manage fisheries, telemetry, and environmental datasets.
·  Process spatial and sonar data and develop maps, tables, figures, and descriptive summaries.
·  Assist with analyses in R or other appropriate software, according to training and project needs.
·  Support reports, data releases, and project documentation; contribute to scientific manuscripts when appropriate to the assigned scope of work.

Expectations by Position Level
B.S.-level position: This is a field-intensive position requiring substantial travel. The selected contractor should expect frequent trips to study sites away from Columbia, including overnight travel and multi-day field assignments, especially during peak field seasons. Responsibilities emphasize high-quality field data collection, equipment maintenance, data management, and collaborative research. Candidates who recently graduated or are finishing a B.S. degree are encouraged to apply.

M.S.-level position: Travel to field sites, including overnight trips, is required, but generally less frequent than for the B.S.-level position. The position may be structured as administrative support or research, depending on the successful candidate’s qualifications and the responsibilities of the award.

·  Administrative-support classification: Emphasis on coordinating project activities, supporting fieldwork, managing and quality-checking data, and preparing technical materials. Independent manuscript development or publication is not expected.
·  Research classification: For candidates with demonstrated analytical and scientific writing skills and an interest in research. Work includes substantive data analysis, interpretation, scientific writing, and development of manuscripts and other research products. Publication depends on project needs and timelines.

Both positions contribute to ongoing team projects. Actual assignments will reflect each individual’s experience and demonstrated skills, the contracted scope of work, and team priorities.

Project Ownership and Professional Development
Both positions offer opportunities to take ownership of components of ongoing projects and develop professionally. Contractors whose assignments include research responsibilities may also contribute to publications and complementary research questions aligned with team objectives. Opportunities to present findings at professional conferences may be available if desired, if funding is available, and if the work aligns with project and team priorities. Catching and banding birds using baited traps and mist nets
Removing pressure geolocator tags from birds
Possibly applying fixed loop geolocator tags on birds 
Collecting and storing fecal samples from birds
Conducting avian point counts
Inputting and proofing data

Outreach to the public

The technician will reside at UGA’s Center for Research and Education at Wormsloe outside of Savannah, Georgia (accessible by car). Description
Position Overview

We are seeking a skilled and passionate Wildlife Biotechnology & Biobanking Technician to join our Memphis Zoo Conservation and Research team to work in reproductive technologies and molecular biology to advance wildlife conservation.

As a core member of our lab, you will managing our biomaterial repository (biobank), conducting biobanking and reproductive research, and assisting with processing and extraction and processing samples for routine molecular assays for qPCR disease testing and enzyme immunoassay. This position reports directly to the Senior Conservation Biologist and offers a unique opportunity to apply cutting-edge biotechnology directly to endangered species preservation.

Essential Job Functions:
Assist with planning and execution of conservation and biobanking research projects, for biobanking genetics of Southeastern endangered snakes and other species as well as coordinate opportunistic biobanking collections during routine physicals exams and post-mortem gamete rescue.
Assist with in situ conservation and research efforts, that may include multi-day trips to Louisiana, Florida, and Mississippi to collect samples from wild-collected snakes for biobanking, data curation and processing, etc.
Assist with ex situ conservation and research efforts, including assisting with monitoring animals for captive-breeding efforts, through disease testing, hormone monitoring, and ultrasound.
 Key Responsibilities
Biobanking & Repository Management
Preserve and catalog diverse biological samples (e.g., tissue, blood, gametes, and cells) from wildlife species.
Maintain cryopreservation equipment (liquid nitrogen tanks, ultra-low freezers) and manage digital inventory database systems.
Ensure strict adherence to quality control, biosafety protocols, and sample tracking standards.
Travel with researchers for collection and biobanking samples at other Zoos and facilities
Reproductive Research & Biotechnology
Support assisted reproductive technology (ART) research, including semen collection techniques, semen analysis, gamete processing, and cryopreservation protocols.
Prepare media, reagents, and specialized equipment for reproductive physiology experiments.
Assist in endocrine monitoring initiatives by performing routine fecal hormone extractions and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs).
Monitor and document experimental outcomes with high precision.
Molecular Biology Support
Perform routine DNA/RNA extractions from a variety of challenging wildlife tissue types.
Run qPCR/PCR assays for disease screening for heard/colony health monitoring and conservation initiatives
Laboratory Operations & Collaboration
Maintain a clean, organized, and safe laboratory environment in coordination with the Lab Manager.
Work with lab manager to maintain laboratory instrumentation.
Collaborate with multidisciplinary teams, including veterinarians, animal care teams, and external conservation partners.
Assist with preparations of permit applications and reports.
Contribute to scientific manuscripts.
Mentor students and volunteers.
Foster a positive, collaborative, safe, and encouraging professional environment.
Perform various duties as assigned.

Experience: Minimum of 1–2 years of hands-on laboratory experience (academic or professional).

Strong record of use and knowledge of reproductive biology techniques (e.g., microscopy, gamete handling)

Experience with basic lab techniques and equipment 
Familiarity with sterile techniques and basic liquid handling.

Experience with DNA/RNA extraction and qPCR/PCR setup

 The Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife (VDFW) is currently recruiting for a Fish and Wildlife Scientist IV position for the role of district habitat biologist and small game project leader.  This position supports a range of critical needs for implementation of wildlife population management, managing small game hunting seasons, and management of Wildlife Management Areas (WMAs) in southeastern Vermont, among other duties to assist other projects.  This is an excellent opportunity for a wildlife professional to make a difference in wildlife conservation in a small state.  This position will work within the Department’s Wildlife Division and be stationed in the Springfield district office.  
 Responsibilities: 
 The Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife is accepting applications from candidates for the position of Fish and Wildlife Scientist IV.  The position is expected to spend 80% of the time coordinating and overseeing the management of Wildlife Management Areas and other state land in the district, and 20% of the time serving as the small game project leader.  The position will be part of the Wildlife Species Management Program of the Wildlife Division within VDFW and coordinate the small game program.  Primary responsibilities are to monitor, manage, and conserve all of Vermont’s small game species.  This responsibility requires coordinating with a variety of different constituents including hunting interests, other state and federal agencies, researchers, and the public.    Outreach and communications with organizations, individuals and government agencies on human-wildlife conflicts is a major task.  Working with division and department administrators on small game hunting regulations and statutes occurs frequently.
 The position will implement and carry out specialized research projects pertaining to small game population estimates, perform necessary disease surveillance, and public opinion surveys.  The position will collect, analyze, and interpret a wide range of biological and social data, submit conclusions to senior staff of the Division and Fish and Wildlife Board, and prepare reports including findings and recommendations based on research projects.  The position will investigate, review, modify, develop, and test new population modeling techniques. The position will participate in the activities of state and interjurisdictional committees and working groups tasked with small game management. 
 This position will plan, coordinate, and oversee the management and administration of Wildlife Management Areas in the Springfield district, in addition to supporting land management efforts on state forests in that district.  This includes conducting and overseeing habitat, natural community, wildlife, historical, and other assessments necessary to plan for the management of WMAs and other state-owned land. This work requires close coordination and partnerships with other state and federal land management agencies, non-government organizations, various stakeholders, and the public. The position will conduct other wildlife management, monitoring, and outreach activities for the wildlife division.  
 The position will work with the program manager to monitor grant activities, budgeting, and reporting related to small game programs.  Complete written federal aid reports in a timely manner.  Serve as the Department’s technical representative with small game technical committees.  Other duties may be assigned including a variety of wildlife inventory and monitoring activities such as woodcock surveys, bald eagle/peregrine falcon/loon nest monitoring, and/or mast surveys.  
 Assist with other wildlife division projects in data collection and outreach.  This includes the operation of moose and deer biological check stations, endangered species monitoring, assistance at public meetings/hearings/events, and outreach events.  
 The Department’s Wildlife Management Program Manager will serve as the official supervisor of this position and provide general guidance, with expectations that the incumbent will exercise significant independent judgement.
